To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the number of queries to a teacher is the most significant factor in determining learning capabilities, and that the type of queries is the second most significant factor.

the number of subset queries can simulate the number of equivalence queries, but a single equivalence query can simulate a finite number of superset and subset queries, but a finite number of equivalence queries cannot simulate a finite number (even one) of superset or subset queries.

(1) the number of queries is a more important measure of learning capabilities than the number of answers; (2) the number of answers is a more important parameter than the types of queries/answers, but the types of queries and the number of answers are not independent parameters; (3) the type of counterexamples is a more important factor than the type of queries/answers.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following questions: What is the minimal number of queries needed for learning a given type of language?

the following questions: 1) what can be learned from positive data and what cannot, 2) what can be done with one query and what requires more, and 3) what can be achieved by different types of queries.

learning languages in the Limit from full positive data with a finite number of equivalence, superset, or subset queries and with a finite number (possibly zero) of counterexamples of different types.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the more the learner is allowed to ask the teacher, the more powerful the learner is.
the more the learner knows, the less it has to query the teacher.
subset queries are more powerful than equivalence queries, but less powerful than superset queries, and superset queries are as powerful as arbitrary queries.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

a finite number of equivalence queries is sufficient to learn languages from full positive data, but a single equivalence query is insufficient to simulate the same finite number of subset or superset queries.
the number of queries is more important than their type.
the number of queries is the most important factor, but the type of queries and counterexamples is not unimportant.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a finite number of positive examples and a finite number, bounded by the number of examples, of queries to the oracle are sufficient to learn languages.
a bounded number of equivalence queries can do much more than a bounded number of subset queries, but a bounded number of superset queries can do much less.
the learning capabilities of a learner depend not only on the number of answers, but also on the types of the answers/counterexamples.
